After: a fifth node E appears in the accent color beside it, with no edges; nothing else changes." width="100%"} This method provides flexible node creation, allowing you to add isolated nodes, nodes with labels, or nodes that are immediately connected to existing nodes. Node IDs are 64-bit unsigned integers managed automatically by EdgeCase, while labels provide human-readable identifiers. IDs are assigned sequentially starting at `1` and are never chosen by the caller. Most other methods accept either an ID or a label wherever a node is expected, so giving nodes unique labels is the most convenient way to work with them. The graph is modified in place and the call is recorded in the step log (see `steps`). Use `add_node()` when building a graph one node at a time, especially when each node needs its own attributes. For many nodes that share a type or attributes, `add_nodes()` is more concise, and generators such as `add_path_graph()` create whole structures in one call. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [label]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional string label for human-readable node access. Non-string values are converted with `str()`, so `add_node(5)` stores the label `"5"`. If `None` (default), the node is unlabelled and can only be referenced by its ID. Labels are unique: a label that another node already has raises a `ValueError`. Keep in mind that methods resolving nodes treat an integer as an ID and a string as a label, so a node labelled `"5"` must be referenced as `"5"`, not `5`. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional string type classification for the node (e.g., `"user"`, `"admin"`, `"organization"`). This is a first-class attribute that always appears as the third column in node DataFrames (with a null value when not set). Default is `None`. [from_node]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[Union[int, str]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional existing node (ID or label) to connect the new node to. Creates an edge pointing from the new node: `new_node -> from_node`. Note that this is the reverse of what the name might suggest. Default is `None` (no edge). [to_node]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[Union[int, str]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional existing node (ID or label) that should point at the new node. Creates an edge `to_node -> new_node`. Can be combined with `from_node=` to create two edges at once. Default is `None` (no edge). In an undirected graph the direction of either edge doesn't matter. [**attributes]{.doc-parameter-name} : Arbitrary key-value pairs to store as node attributes (e.g., `age=30`, `role="engineer"`). Each key becomes a column in the node DataFrame; nodes that don't have a given attribute show a null value in that column. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Returns self to enable method chaining. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [NodeNotFoundError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `from_node=` or `to_node=` refers to a node that doesn't exist. Nothing is added. [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If another node already has this label. Nothing is added. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Calling `add_node()` with just a label creates an isolated node and returns the graph for chaining; look up its auto-assigned ID afterward with `get_id_from_label()`: ::: {#d16f3a6e .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_node(label="Node1") graph.get_id_from_label("Node1") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 1 ``` ::: ::: Because `add_node()` returns `self`, a whole graph can be assembled as one chained expression: ::: {#a33e63cc .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_node(label="Alice") .add_node(label="Bob") .add_node(label="Charlie") ) graph ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` Number of nodes : 3 Number of edges : 0 Directed : False Density : 0.00 Average degree (min, max) : 0.00 (0, 0) Connected : False Number of connected components : 3 Tree : False Bipartite : True ``` ::: ::: Passing `from_node=` or `to_node=` connects the new node to an existing one in the same call, saving a separate `add_edge()` step. The edge list (as source/target labels) shows that `from_node=` makes the new node the source and `to_node=` makes it the target: ::: {#eeb130e1 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_node(label="Alice") .add_node(label="Bob", from_node="Alice") # edge: Bob -> Alice .add_node(label="Charlie", to_node="Alice") # edge: Alice -> Charlie ) [ (graph.get_label_from_id(src), graph.get_label_from_id(tgt)) for src, tgt in zip(graph.get_edge_df()["source"], graph.get_edge_df()["target"]) ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` [('Bob', 'Alice'), ('Alice', 'Charlie')] ``` ::: ::: `type=` and any other keyword arguments are stored as node attributes, each becoming a column of the node DataFrame. Nodes lacking an attribute get a null in that column: ::: {#ca87fe98 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_node(label="Alice", type="person", age=30, role="engineer") .add_node(label="Bob", type="person", age=25) ) graph.get_node_df() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
